content.title: Closest Binary Search Tree Value II

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a BST, a target value, and an integer k, return the k values in the BST closest to target. The result may be returned in any order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"K closest values to a target, in a BST\"","In-order traversal gives sorted values; this reduces exactly to Find K Closest Elements"],["A sorted array plus a target","Binary search for the best window of k consecutive values"]]}

blocks.text: Once the BST is flattened via in-order traversal into a sorted array, this problem is IDENTICAL to Find K Closest Elements: the k closest values to a target in a sorted array always form a contiguous window, found via binary search.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the k Closest Prices in an Already-Sorted Price List
blocks.text: Picture a price list already sorted, and wanting the k prices closest to a target price. Since the list is sorted, those k prices always form one continuous stretch, found by binary searching for where that stretch should begin.

blocks.caption: In-order traversal flattens the BST to sorted values, reducing this to Find K Closest Elements

blocks.text: Result: [3, 4]. In-order gives [1,2,3,4,5]; the window [3,4] is closest to 3.714.

Before scanning the tree for the closest values directly, notice that in-order traversal produces a sorted array, and the k closest values to a target in ANY sorted array always form a contiguous window, solvable via the same binary search technique as Find K Closest Elements.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In-order traversal of a BST always produces its values in sorted order, regardless of tree shape.

Observation 2: In a sorted array, the k values closest to a target always form ONE contiguous window, since anything outside that window is provably farther from target than something at the window's edge.

Observation 3: Binary searching for the correct starting index of this window (comparing the distance from target to the window's potential new left edge versus the value it would drop from the right) finds the answer in O(log(n-k)).

Observation 4: This is EXACTLY the Find K Closest Elements technique, applied after flattening the BST via in-order traversal.

This leads to: flatten the BST via in-order traversal into a sorted array, then binary search for the best window of k consecutive values closest to target (same technique as Find K Closest Elements).
Collect all values via traversal, sort them by their distance to target, and take the first k.
Why the code is written this way

items: Sorting by distance directly finds the k closest values, correct regardless of tree structure.
This costs O(n log n), ignoring that in-order traversal already gives sorted values, enabling a much faster binary search.

blocks.text: Limitation: flattening via in-order traversal (already O(n)) then binary searching for the best window achieves O(n + log(n-k)) overall.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Flatten the BST via in-order traversal into a sorted array (O(n)). Then, exactly as in Find K Closest Elements, binary search for the window's starting index: compare the distance from target to the window's potential new left edge against the value it would drop from the right, narrowing the search accordingly.
In-order traversal to get sorted values; binary search for the best window of k consecutive values using the Find K Closest Elements technique.
Dry run for values=[1,2,3,4,5], target=3.714286, k=2

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) for the traversal, O(log(n-k)) for the binary search.
Space: O(n) for the values array.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "k closest values to a target, in a BST", think: flatten via in-order traversal, apply the Find K Closest Elements binary search.

items: How would you solve this using two stacks (predecessor/successor pointers) without flattening the whole tree, for O(k + log n) instead?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Sorting by distance costs O(n log n) time; the in-order-flatten-plus-binary-search approach costs O(n + log(n-k)) time, both using O(n) space.

items: Pattern: flatten via in-order traversal, then apply the Find K Closest Elements binary search technique.
Core Idea: the k closest values to a target in a sorted array always form a contiguous window, found via binary search on the window's start.
Time: O(n log n) for sorting by distance, O(n + log(n-k)) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: in-order traversal reduces this BST problem directly to the classic Find K Closest Elements problem.
Interview Difficulty: a satisfying reduction problem connecting BST traversal to a previously-seen binary search technique.
